MTAM encodes elapsed time as δ=tanh(Wδ·log1p(Δt)+bδ), combines it with a tanh-transformed input/hidden-state context, then applies a sigmoid temporal gate. Its T-GRU multiplies the retained-history term by this gate; it does not add an offset to the update-gate logits. The temporal gate is bounded, but its trainable weights are unconstrained: bounded intermediate features alone do not bound a subsequent logit offset. MTAM also reports no obvious improvement from enforcing exponential time decay, cautioning against assuming temporal relevance must decrease monotonically. [MTAM paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2005.08598)

A reproducible bounded-offset variant—an engineering proposal, not MTAM’s published parameterization—is z=σ(a_z+o), with o=A·tanh(v)·f(Δt), fixed A, and bounded f. For example, f=tanh(log1p(Δt/u)/s), using explicit time unit u and a positive scale s fixed from training histories. This guarantees |o|≤A; an unconstrained learned multiplier outside tanh would remove that guarantee. Normalization should precede tanh: large arguments saturate and make distinct intervals nearly indistinguishable. Log1p already compresses large gaps, so inspect training-gap quantiles before choosing s.

Represent timestamp availability explicitly; an unknown gap should not silently become an observed zero gap. GRU-D supports the broader principle of supplying observation masks alongside elapsed-time features, although its evidence concerns clinical missingness rather than missing recommendation timestamps. For this adaptation, use a valid-gap indicator, neutralize the temporal offset when either endpoint is unavailable, and keep padding separate. Compute features only from observed history timestamps and preserve their scaling in the checkpoint and predictor. [GRU-D paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-24271-9)
